transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-01-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luis Carvalho (Redwood SE), Mark Dawson (Helios CTO), Leah Kim (Helios Head of Platform), Omar Ruiz (Helios Sr Engineer), Sana Patel (Helios PM)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for blocking time, appreciate it. Quick intros then we'll get into scope.
[00:18] Mark: Hey, Mark here, CTO at Helios. We're building a commerce assistant that touches checkout, product search, and merchant dashboards. Main goal is to reduce friction on cart conversions.
[00:28] Leah: Leah, I own the platform and infra side — interested in operational characteristics and security.
[00:35] Jordan: Great, Priya, Luis on the call to talk tech and benchmarks.
[00:40] Priya: Hi all — we'll focus on API patterns, OpenAI-compat endpoints, function/tool calling for live inventory checks, and structured output so downstream systems can ingest responses reliably.
[00:52] Sana: Quick note — success metrics for us are p95 latency under 350ms for short prompts in checkout flows, and cost per completed checkout under $0.05 in model runtime if possible. Also need deterministic structured JSON outputs for product suggestions.
[01:12] Luis: Okay interesting, that helps a lot. Can you give us rough workload numbers? concurrent users, average tokens per request, bursts?
[01:22] Mark: Typical peak is about 1200 reqs/minute across our edge, bursts to 2500 for promos. Most checkout prompts are ~40-120 tokens, some longer context for product recommendations up to 600 tokens.
[01:38] Omar: And we do a lot of enrichment calls — lookup to inventory, price calc, A/B rules — so we need function/tool calling so the model can ask for live lookup rather than rely on hallucinated prices.
[01:52] Priya: Good, so two main patterns: 1) short single-shot prompts for checkout suggestions (low tokens, high qps), 2) longer context sessions for multi-turn product discovery. We'll propose different model variants and batching configs.
[02:10] Jordan: For the POC, proposed success criteria listed — baseline p95 < 400ms for checkout path, 99.9% availability during test window, and less than 15% regression in conversion compared to current heuristics — does that align?
[02:28] Sana: That's reasonable. Also need clear regressions detection in structured output (schema mismatches).
[02:35] Mark: And security — we need KMS for keys and audit logs exported to our SIEM. SOC2 compliance is a must.
[02:46] Priya: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS in Private deployments and has audit logging and integration paths for SIEM. For hosted, we can provide detailed logs with redaction and retention policies — we'll share specifics.
[03:02] Mark: If we go with hosted initially, we need guarantees around data handling and geolocation — EU data residency for some merchants.
[03:12] Luis: We can route workloads by region and pin model variants to region; for the POC we can emulate EU-resident traffic in our test harness.
[03:25] Jordan: Let's dig into integration — Helios uses Node.js mid-tier and a small Python ML platform. Preferred integration is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so we can reuse existing client libs.
[03:37] Priya: Redwood has OpenAI-compatible endpoints and SDKs for Python and Node. We support both the chat and completions shapes, plus function calling. For function/tool calling you can register RPC-like tool definitions; the runtime will call back to your endpoint for inventory/price lookups.
[03:58] Omar: How does auth look? We need SSO for engineer access, and per-route API keys ideally mapped to environments.
[04:07] Luis: We integrate with SSO/SAML for Console and have API key management for the runtime; RBAC can limit keys to dev/stage/prod.
[04:17] Omar: Great. On tool calling, what about latency when the model invokes a tool? If it waits synchronously for inventory it could blow past p95.
[04:27] Priya: Good question. Pattern we recommend: keep tool responses small and cacheable; for critical checkout calls we use an inline fast lookup service or pre-warm cache. Also Redwood supports KV cache to stash recent lookups, and we can configure fallbacks — model asks tool, if timeout use cached safe value. We'll include an example flow in the playbook.
[04:52] Mark: Sounds sensible. For structured output: we need strict JSON with schema validation and a fallback string when schema fails. Can Redwood enforce schema at the runtime?
[05:04] Priya: We do post-response validation hooks and can apply JSON schema checks; when validation fails, policies can trigger a re-roll, call a fallback tool, or return an error object. We also support function-like structured responses (name/arguments) so you can map fields directly.
[05:22] Sana: We want deterministic slot filling for product_id, price, and availability boolean. No hallucinated price.
[05:29] Luis: We'll recommend model variants that are tuned for structured outputs and lower hallucination. Also provide prompt templates and eval harness to verify schema adherence over your prompt set.
[05:44] Jordan: Benchmarks — Priya, outline our recommended benchmark approach.
[05:48] Priya: We'll run two benchmark tracks: steady-state throughput to measure cost/token and tail latency, and burst rounds to validate autoscaling and fallbacks. We'll include a synthetic corpus based on your real prompts (anonymized) and hit the OpenAI-compatible endpoint with realistic token distributions. Key metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, error rates, and schema pass-rate.
[06:18] Mark: For the POC window — how long should the benchmark and pilot run? We're aiming to sign by end of quarter.
[06:25] Jordan: Typical POC is 3 weeks: 1 week integration + test harness, 1 week benchmark and tuning, 1 week pilot in staging with real traffic. We can compress but prefer 3 weeks to collect statistically meaningful data.
[06:38] Leah: We need to align with our SRE calendar — can't do heavy load tests on the 27th because of infra maintenance.
[06:45] Jordan: Noted. We'll coordinate dates in the next steps.
[06:50] Omar: A couple of technical details — do you support streaming token responses? We use streaming in checkout to improve perceived latency.
[06:58] Priya: Yes, we support streaming for both chat and completions shapes, and you can integrate with your websockets or SSE layer. Streaming doesn't change backend batching semantics much but improves UX.
[07:14] Mark: And model variants — are there quantized options to cut cost? We care about cost per checkout.
[07:20] Luis: We can recommend INT8 quantized variants or smaller family models for the short prompt checkout path. Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization and batching configurations based on your token distribution.
[07:34] Sana: We also want to try a fallback plan: primary low-latency model, fallback to cheaper variant if cost or capacity thresholds triggered, and a degrade-path that returns cached deterministic recommendations.
[07:46] Priya: Those routing policies are supported; we can set threshold-based automatic fallback by latency or capacity. We'll document a canary rollout for any model changes.
[07:58] Jordan: For the benchmark environment, who on your side will own pairing infra/network?
[08:04] Leah: Omar and I will coordinate; we'll provide an env with anonymized traffic and a staging API gateway.
[08:12] Priya: We'll need service endpoints for your inventory and price lookup if we test tool calling end-to-end; alternatively you can provide a mocked tool that mirrors latencies.
[08:24] Omar: We'll mock for the first run and then open a secure tunnel for a live lookup test in week 2.
[08:30] Mark: What about observability — request tracing, token-level cost, and per-route dashboards?
[08:36] Luis: Redwood Console will give per-route latency and token breakdowns, and exportable traces. We can also send logs to your SIEM or S3 bucket.
[08:46] Sana: Need to confirm data retention and redaction capabilities for exported logs.
[08:51] Priya: We'll include retention options in the security deck and can redact user PII before export.
[08:58] Mark: Any blockers we should be aware of?
[09:02] Jordan: Biggest potential blockers: data residency for EU traffic, SOC2 paperwork and legal SLRs, and any on-prem requirement. If those crop up, the Private deployment path is available but takes longer.
[09:15] Leah: On-prem would require procurement sign-off and longer timelines; prefer hosted for the POC if compliance docs are sufficient.
[09:23] Jordan: We'll send SOC2 summary and KMS options asap.
[09:28] Priya: On the technical side, we'll prepare a benchmark script (Node + Python runners), sample prompt corpus, and example schema enforcement rules.
[09:38] Sana: For success criteria let's restate explicitly: 1) p95 latency < 400ms for checkout short prompts, 2) schema pass-rate > 98% for structured outputs, 3) cost per completed checkout < $0.05, 4) no data exfil observed in logs.
[09:58] Jordan: Good, we'll include those in the playbook as acceptance criteria.
[10:05] Mark: Curious about pricing for Dedicated vs hosted during POC — we want to ensure predictable costs during load testing.
[10:13] Jordan: For POC load tests we typically use hosted with committed test credits and a short term Dedicated reservation if you want dedicated GPUs for consistent p95 numbers. We'll send a pricing comparison in the worksheet.
[10:30] Omar: If we need to run a real-time tool call to inventory that can return transient errors, how does Redwood handle retries and idempotency?
[10:38] Luis: Retry policies are configurable: upstream tool calls can be retried with exponential backoff; we suggest idempotency tokens on your side for mutating calls. For read lookups we recommend short cache TTLs and circuit-breaker patterns.
[10:54] Priya: Also for function calling we can surface tool errors in structured error fields so your mid-tier can decide fallback logic.
[11:05] Sana: One more ask — can we have a preflight run where you simulate malicious prompts or prompt injection attempts against our schemas?
[11:14] Priya: Yes, we include prompt-safety tests and adversarial prompts in the eval harness; we can run those against your schema and show failure modes.
[11:26] Jordan: Ok wrapping up — recap of immediate next steps: Jordan shares POC playbook + pricing; Priya shares benchmark scripts and sample corpus; Helios provides traffic and prompt samples + compliance contact; schedule benchmark kickoff for 2026-01-20.
[11:44] Mark: Sounds good. We'll aim to have the traffic sample and compliance contact by 2026-01-19.
[11:50] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow-up with calendar invites and shared drive links.
